title: Reading the Didache

objectives.can: Read the Didache's Two Ways: imperatives, future used as command, and vocabulary shared with Matthew.

explanation.summary: The Didache is a short Christian handbook in plain Greek, probably from the late first or the second century (scholars disagree on the date). Its opening chapters, the Two Ways, are made of commands, and they share sayings with the Gospel of Matthew and the Gospel of Luke.

sections.heading: Before you read: the text is analysed by machine
body: The Greek of the Didache in this library has been analysed by a program, and no one has checked the analysis word by word. The New Testament, by contrast, was checked by hand. So on this page, and in the other Apostolic Father and Athanasius lessons, a lemma or a grammatical label can be wrong or missing.

You will see a few words in the Didache text without any analysis at all. A few others carry a label that a Greek reader would correct (for example, a participle labelled as if it were a finite verb). The lesson therefore picks examples whose analysis is reliable, and its questions are written by hand. When the program and the grammar disagree, trust the grammar.

sections.heading: Two ways of commanding
body: The Two Ways material gives commands in two forms. One is the imperative, the form you learned for direct commands: εὐλογεῖτε, 'bless', προσεύχεσθε, 'pray', ὕπαγε, 'go', δὸς, 'give'. The negative command (the prohibition) uses μή with the present imperative, as in μὴ ἀπαίτει, 'do not ask back', or with an aorist subjunctive.

The other form is the future indicative used as a command. οὐ φονεύσεις, 'you shall not murder', is grammatically a statement, 'you will not murder', but it is heard as a rule. Ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν, 'you shall love your neighbour as yourself', does the same in the positive. This usage is a mark of legal and commandment language. The New Testament has it too, where it quotes the commandments: Matthew 19:18 and Romans 13:9 both contain οὐ φονεύσεις. Many scholars connect it with the way the Greek translation of the Law renders Hebrew commandments, and the Didache's Two Ways are close to that wording; this is a view about origins, not something the grammar proves.

sections.heading: Conditions and 'those who …'
body: The Didache's rules for conduct are often built from ἐάν with the subjunctive: ἐάν τίς σοι δῷ ῥάπισμα, 'if anyone gives you a blow'. This is the ordinary form of an open condition about something that may happen. The main clause is then a command: στρέψον αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν ἄλλην.

The Didache also names people by articular participles, as the Gospels do: τοὺς ἀγαπῶντας ὑμᾶς, 'those who love you', and ὁ μὴ χρείαν ἔχων, 'the one who has no need'. Read the article and the participle together as a noun phrase, and the participle's own object or adverb stays inside it.

sections.heading: Vocabulary shared with Matthew and Luke
body: Didache 1.3–5 overlaps with the Sermon on the Mount and the Sermon on the Plain. The saying about the blow on the right cheek shares its closing words (στρέψον αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν ἄλλην) with Matthew 5:39, though the opening differs, and ὕπαγε μετ' αὐτοῦ δύο matches Matthew 5:41. The question 'what grace is it if you love those who love you?' is built on the phrasing of Luke 6:32 (ποία ὑμῖν χάρις ἐστίν), where Matthew 5:46 has μισθός instead of χάρις.

The words alone do not tell you which text came first, whether the Didache borrowed from the Gospels, or whether both drew on a common stream of teaching. Scholars hold different views on this. For reading, what matters is that you can recognise a familiar saying in slightly different words.

sections.heading: The style of this Greek
body: The sentences are short and the word order is plain. Particles such as δέ, γάρ and οὖν hold the commands together. The vocabulary is mostly that of the New Testament: ἐντολή, 'commandment', διδαχή, 'teaching', χάρις, 'grace' or 'credit', ὁδός, 'way'. Because the text is built from commands and conditions, the whole passage can be read with the verb forms you already know.

misunderstandings: A future verb with οὐ is not a prediction. In commandment language οὐ φονεύσεις means 'you shall not murder'. Read the context, not the tense label alone.
μὴ ποίει is not 'you will not do': with μή, a present imperative is a prohibition, 'do not do'.
χάρις does not always mean 'grace' in a theological sense. In ποία γὰρ χάρις it asks what credit or thanks is due, as in Luke 6:32.
Do not trust every label in the Didache's analysis. It is automatic; if a form looks wrong, check it against the grammar.

deeper.heading: The Two Ways as a pattern
body: The Way of Life and the Way of Death are not unique to the Didache: the Epistle of Barnabas, also in this library, has a related Two Ways section, and scholars have long discussed how the two texts relate and whether both used an earlier source. Comparing the two is a good exercise once you can read either one with confidence.

quoted.title: Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
quoted.english: The Way of Life is this: First, thou shalt love the God who made thee, secondly, thy neighbour as thyself; and whatsoever thou wouldst not have done to thyself, do not thou to another.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon

examples.analysis: ἀγαπήσεις is future indicative, second person singular: 'you shall love'. It stands for a command. θελήσῃς is an aorist subjunctive, second person singular, after ἐάν: 'whatever you may wish not to happen to you'. ποίει is a present imperative, second person singular, with μή before it: the negative form of the golden rule, 'do not do to another'.

quoted.title: Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
quoted.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon

examples.analysis: A series of commands and conditions. ἀπέχου is a present imperative (middle form), 'keep away from', with a genitive of what you avoid. δῷ is an aorist subjunctive after ἐάν, 'if anyone gives'. στρέψον, ὕπαγε and δός are the commands of the main clauses: 'turn', 'go', 'give'. Aorist imperatives (στρέψον, δὸς) and a present imperative (ὕπαγε) stand side by side.

examples.analysis: Matthew 5:41 has the same command as Didache 1.4, ὕπαγε μετ' αὐτοῦ δύο, 'go with him two'. Matthew's condition uses a future indicative, ἀγγαρεύσει, 'will compel', where the Didache has ἐάν and a subjunctive. The two texts share words but not every construction.

reading.reference: Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles) 1.2 – Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles) 1.5
reading.why: Four sections of the Way of Life: commands, a future that commands, ἐάν clauses and articular participles, with sayings you can set beside Matthew 5 and Luke 6. Remember that the program's analysis may mislead you in places.

segments.title: Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
segments.english: The Way of Life is this: First, thou shalt love the God who made thee, secondly, thy neighbour as thyself; and whatsoever thou wouldst not have done to thyself, do not thou to another.
segments.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon

segments.title: Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
segments.english: Now, the teaching of these words is this: Bless those that curse you, and pray for your enemies, and fast for those that persecute you. For what credit is it to you if you love those that love you? Do not even the heathen do the same? But, for your part, love those that hate you, and you will have no enemy.
segments.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon

segments.title: Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
segments.english: Abstain from carnal and bodily lusts. If any man smite thee on the right cheek, turn to him the other cheek also, and thou wilt be perfect. If any man impress thee to go with him one mile, go with him two. If any man take thy coat, give him thy shirt also. If any man will take from thee what is thine, refuse it not—not even if thou canst.
segments.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon

segments.title: Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
segments.english: Give to everyone that asks thee, and do not refuse, for the Father’s will is that we give to all from the gifts we have received. Blessed is he that gives according to the mandate; for he is innocent. Woe to him who receives; for if any man receive alms under pressure of need he is innocent; but he who receives it without need shall be tried as to why he took and for what, and being in prison he shall be examined as to his deeds, and he shall not come out thence until he pay the last farthing.
segments.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon
